statement: To a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.
heath_proof: Let AB be the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let BC be an annex to AB; therefore AC, CB are straight lines incommensurable in square which fulfil the given conditions. [X. 77] I say that no other straight line can be annexed to AB which fulfils the same conditions. For, if possible, let BD be so annexed; therefore AD, DB are also straight lines incommensurable in square which fulfil the given conditions. [X. 77] Since then, as in the preceding cases, the excess of the squares on AD, DB over the squares on AC, CB is also the excess of twice the rectangle AD, DB over twice the rectangle AC, CB, while twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by a rational area, for both are rational, therefore the squares on AD, DB also exceed the squares on AC, CB by a rational area: which is impossible, for both are medial. [X. 26] Therefore no other straight line can be annexed to AB which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole fulfils the aforesaid conditions; therefore only one straight line can be so annexed.

10.83
**Statement:** To a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let CB be annexed to it, so that AC is the whole and AB = AC - CB. Then by the definition of this irrational line (10.77), AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial, and twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB is rational.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that another straight line BD, different from CB, can also be annexed to AB so that AD is the whole and AB = AD - DB, with AD and DB satisfying the same conditions: AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD and DB is medial, and twice the rectangle contained by AD and DB is rational.

**Step 3.** Since twice the rectangle AC.CB is rational, and twice the rectangle AD.DB is also rational, these two areas are commensurable with one another, for rational areas are commensurable with one another (D10.1.4, 10.12).

**Step 4.** Now, by 2.7, the square on AC equals the sum of the square on AB, the square on CB, and twice the rectangle AB.CB. Therefore twice the rectangle AC.CB equals the square on AC minus the square on CB minus the square on AB, rearranging. More precisely, the squares on AC and CB together equal the square on AB plus twice the rectangle AC.CB (by 2.7 applied to AC = AB + CB: sq(AC) = sq(AB) + sq(CB) + 2*rect(AB,CB), so sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AB) + 2*sq(CB) + 2*rect(AB,CB)). Let us proceed more directly.

**Step 5.** By 2.7, since AC = AB + BC, we have the square on AC equal to the squares on AB and BC together with twice the rectangle AB.BC. Similarly, since AD = AB + BD, the square on AD equals the squares on AB and BD together with twice the rectangle AB.BD.

**Step 6.** Therefore the squares on AC and CB taken together equal the square on AB plus two times the square on CB plus twice the rectangle AB.CB, which by rearrangement gives: sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AB) + 2*sq(CB) + 2*rect(AB,CB). Likewise, sq(AD) + sq(DB) = sq(AB) + 2*sq(DB) + 2*rect(AB,DB).

**Step 7.** Now twice the rectangle AC.CB is rational and twice the rectangle AD.DB is rational, so by subtraction: [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - 2*rect(AC,CB) = sq(AB) = [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] - 2*rect(AD,DB). This means sq(AC) + sq(CB) - 2*rect(AC,CB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB) - 2*rect(AD,DB).

**Step 8.** Therefore [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] = 2*rect(AC,CB) - 2*rect(AD,DB) (CN2, CN3).

**Step 9.** The left side, [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - [sq(AD) + sq(DB)], is the difference of two medial areas (since both sums of squares are medial by hypothesis). The right side, 2*rect(AC,CB) - 2*rect(AD,DB), is the difference of two rational areas (since both double rectangles are rational by hypothesis).

**Step 10.** If the left side is not zero, then a medial area exceeds (or falls short of) a medial area by a rational area, which contradicts 10.26, which states that a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area.

**Step 11.** Therefore the left side must be zero: sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB). And consequently the right side must also be zero: 2*rect(AC,CB) = 2*rect(AD,DB).

**Step 12.** Since sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB), and also 2*rect(AC,CB) = 2*rect(AD,DB), we add these equalities: [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] + 2*rect(AC,CB) = [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] + 2*rect(AD,DB). By 2.4, the left side equals the square on (AC + CB) and the right side equals the square on (AD + DB). Therefore the square on (AC + CB) equals the square on (AD + DB), whence AC + CB = AD + DB (CN1).

**Step 13.** Similarly, by subtraction: [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - 2*rect(AC,CB) = [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] - 2*rect(AD,DB). By 2.7, the left side equals the square on (AC - CB) and the right side equals the square on (AD - DB). But AC - CB = AB = AD - DB. So this is consistent and holds automatically.

**Step 14.** From Step 12, AC + CB = AD + DB. From the hypothesis, AC - CB = AB = AD - DB. Adding these two equations: 2*AC = 2*AD, so AC = AD (CN2, CN1). Subtracting: 2*CB = 2*DB, so CB = DB.

**Step 15.** Therefore the same straight line CB is annexed, and no other line BD different from CB can satisfy the conditions. This proves that to a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the sum of squares medial but twice the rectangle rational. Q.E.D.
